name: Myrtle (Myrtus communis) applied in the mouth
short: Mouth paste (45 people): no side effects reported. Skin trials: side effects as often as comparators. Vaginal gel, suppository and syrup abstracts give no safety data; nor for children or pregnancy.
text: This entry is built for myrtle (Myrtus communis) paste applied to mouth ulcers; it is not about lemon myrtle or wax myrtle, which are other plants. In a randomised, double-blind trial in 45 people with recurrent aphthous stomatitis who used a placebo paste and a myrtle paste in two consecutive ulcer episodes, no side effects were reported. A 2016 review states that myrtle essential oil and decoction reduced ulcer size and pain in minor aphthous stomatitis without any adverse effects. Applied to the skin (a different route): in a 55-person split-face acne trial against clindamycin, a 90-person dandruff trial against ketoconazole and a 100-person, four-group wart trial of myrtle, alone or with Descurainia sophia, against salicylic acid, alone or with Descurainia sophia (the abstract calls myrtle a topical treatment but does not say how Descurainia sophia was given; its results call the frequency of side effects similar, while its conclusion says myrtle had fewer side effects), the frequency of side effects did not differ significantly between myrtle and the comparator, or was similar (the abstracts do not say what the side effects were). Other forms: the abstracts of trials of myrtle extract mixed into a metronidazole vaginal gel, of a myrtle vaginal suppository (60 women), and of myrtle fruit syrup taken by mouth by children aged 1 to 7 with reflux report no adverse-event data, so no safety statement can be made for those forms or for children. The cited sources report no cases of allergy and give no data on pregnancy. No interaction data were found in the cited sources.
